text.en: Asha clapped near the hill behind her school and heard her clap again a moment later. "That is an echo," said her teacher.

Sound is produced by vibrating bodies and needs a medium to travel, so it cannot pass through a vacuum. In air, sound travels as a longitudinal wave. The air particles move back and forth along the direction the wave travels, producing compressions and rarefactions. The speed of sound is different in solids, liquids and gases.
A sound wave has a time period, a frequency (vibrations per second), a wavelength, an amplitude and a speed. Larger pressure variations can make a sound louder under comparable conditions. Pitch is strongly related to frequency. Timbre helps distinguish sounds at the same pitch and loudness.
Sound with a frequency below 20 Hz is infrasonic and above 20,000 Hz is ultrasonic. Sound can reflect from a firm surface. A separate echo is often distinguishable when the reflected sound arrives about a tenth of a second or more after the direct sound. Reverberation is the persistence of sound from repeated reflections.
Ultrasonic sound is used in SONAR to find the depth of the sea and in medical scans, and the electrocardiogram records the electrical activity of the heart.

Pluck a stretched band gently and watch it move to and fro. A nearby piece of tissue can show movement when air is disturbed. The original vibration starts the sound.
In a diagram of sound travelling through air, one particle does not travel from the source to your ear. Neighbouring particles pass on the disturbance as they move around their usual positions.
A compression is a region where air particles are temporarily closer together. In a rarefaction they are farther apart. Both regions move along as the pressure pattern travels.
In a vacuum chamber diagram, the electric bell can keep vibrating as air is removed. The airborne sound reaching the listener weakens because there is less air to carry the pressure wave.
A pressure-versus-position graph may show a wave with peaks and troughs. These depict pressure changes. Air particles in a sound wave do not move up and down like the graph’s outline.
Find one wavelength by measuring from one compression to the next compression. On the pressure sketch, the distance from one peak to the next represents that same repeat distance.

board.text: Wavelength λ: compression to next compression

text.en: Frequency counts repeats each second. A five hundred hertz vibration makes five hundred cycles in one second. The time for one cycle is one divided by five hundred seconds.
Amplitude is the size of a maximum departure from an average value. For the same frequency and listening setup, a larger pressure amplitude usually makes the sound louder.

board.text: Compare amplitudes at the same frequency

text.en: Now keep amplitude similar and compare sounds with frequencies two hundred and four hundred hertz. The four hundred hertz tone has the higher pitch.
Instruments with the same main pitch can sound different as their mixtures of vibration frequencies and their attacks differ. This difference in sound quality is part of timbre.
A sound wave moves one wavelength in one period. Dividing wavelength by period gives speed. As period is the reciprocal of frequency, speed equals frequency times wavelength.
For five hundred hertz and a wavelength of zero point six eight metres, multiply to find a speed of three hundred forty metres per second.
Sound speed depends on the medium and its temperature. It is often much greater in solid steel than in ordinary air, and generally greater in warmer air than in cooler air.

board.text: Speed depends on the material and its conditions

text.en: Human hearing is often described as about twenty hertz to twenty thousand hertz, though the limits vary. Below that range is infrasound and above it is ultrasound.
A flat reflector can send some sound back. In a ray sketch, draw a normal at the surface to compare incoming and outgoing angles, as for reflection of light.

board.text: Reflection angles are measured from the normal

text.en: For an echo, trace the path out to the wall and back to the source. At three hundred forty metres per second and a delay of zero point two seconds, the total travel is sixty-eight metres.
If the source and receiver are in the same place, the wall is thirty-four metres away. Divide by two because both travel legs were counted in the measured delay.
Many close reflections can blend with the direct sound and each other in a hall. This is reverberation. Suitable soft or porous finishes can absorb some sound and reduce its persistence.
A horn can direct sound by reflection. A stethoscope guides body sounds to the listener. These are examples of devices that manage sound paths.

board.text: Devices can guide sound along useful paths

text.en: Sonar uses the time of a returning sound pulse to estimate underwater distances. Use the speed in water and allow for travel in both directions.

board.text: Echo sounding uses the speed in water

text.en: Medical ultrasound imaging uses returning high-frequency sound to form images. An electrocardiogram instead records electrical signals from the heart. The two measurements use different kinds of signals.
To compare two sounds, identify which quantity changed first. Use frequency for pitch, waveform and timing for timbre, and the travel path and delay for an echo problem.

board.text: Match the observation to the physical quantity

problem.en: An echo returns after 0.20 s. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. Find the one-way distance to the wall.

text.en: Multiply three hundred forty metres per second by zero point two seconds.

why.en: The full sound path is sixty-eight metres.

text.en: Halve the full path length.

why.en: Both the outward and return paths are counted, so the wall is thirty-four metres away.

prompt.en: A friend says Sound can travel through a vacuum. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Sound needs a medium of particles.
In a vacuum there is nothing to vibrate.

points.en: Sound needs a medium. In air it travels as a longitudinal wave.
Loudness depends on amplitude, pitch on frequency.
